task_brief: This is day 1 of "Productivity and Collaboration Tools". That is unit 3 in grade 4. Today is a diagnostic probe about efficient typing practice. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Create an accessible one-page document or short slide set on a class topic. Today helps by working on efficient typing practice. Your unit also covers efficient typing practice, formatting a document, building a simple slide, and using accessibility features. Today is for practice. You are scored on finishing and being honest, not on getting it perfect.
primary_task: First, write what you already think about efficient typing practice. Do this before anyone explains it. Draw or list the steps you think are needed. Then guess one thing that would break your steps. Try your steps on two examples you make up. Mark what worked. Mark what did not. A wrong guess is fine here. It does not lower your score. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about efficient typing practice. It is part of "Productivity and Collaboration Tools". Later days in this unit cover other things, like formatting a document. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about efficient typing practice; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 4, try the steps yourself before you ask for help. Give a reason in your own words for at least one choice. A labelled drawing or a spoken answer counts fully.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task names a hand or body skill (efficient typing practice) as the thing being learned. If that is hard for you, you may use a different way instead — one hand, a switch, voice typing, a bigger or different mouse, eye control, or an adult typing while you say the answer. Using a different way is worth full marks.
You can do this with the keyboard only, no mouse needed. Text can be made bigger, and you may do it on paper instead of a screen.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, API key, or identifiable image.
Use only fictional or sandboxed systems, accounts, and data; never probe, exploit, or attempt to access a real external system.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify, not as an authority or a substitute for learner work.
The tutor may explain, demonstrate, or debug alongside the learner, but must not silently complete a graded project or assessment for them.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting efficient typing practice.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for efficient typing practice follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for efficient typing practice, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for efficient typing practice works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of efficient typing practice, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking efficient typing practice mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply efficient typing practice under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on efficient typing practice rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
